div.p: In the previous chapter, we posited an equivalence between Crowleyan occult-style Sex Magick and the libertine lifestyle of certain segments of the British pre-war upper class, which we called practical sex magic. We provided some circumstantial evidence to support this equivalence claim, such as the overlap between the two social circles and the language used by Beat Generation authors, but this is hardly enough. We will now substantiate our claim that this equivalence corresponds to a concrete reality, based on René Girard's frameworks of mimetic desire and metaphysical desire.

div.head: 3.1 Girardian desire
div.p: The foundation of René Girard's theoretical framework, as originally formulated in his analysis of the European novel, begins with a deceptively simple geometric observation regarding human longing. Traditionally, romantic and philosophical thought has conceptualized desire as a linear dynamic consisting of two points: a desiring subject and a desired object. In this prevailing romantic illusion, as Girard puts it, the subject believes their desire is entirely spontaneous and autonomous, originating from within their own authentic self and directed toward an object whose inherent qualities naturally draw them in. Girard shatters this dyadic model by introducing a third point, the mediator or model, thus forming a triangle. According to this triangular configuration, the subject does not actually desire the object for its own sake; rather, the subject desires the object because it is already desired—or possessed—by the mediator. Consequently, all desireIn DD&TN, the phrase all desire, must be considered with prudence. Of course, Girard does not pretend that a desire to run to the toilet is imitated from a mediator. However, he insists on repeating all because he wants to warn the reader that the number of desires motivated by imitation is always greater than we acknowledge of realize. is inherently borrowed, constituting what is known as mimetic desire.

The relationship between the subject and the mediator dictates the intensity and the destructive potential of this imitative process. When the mediator is socially, historically, or culturally distant from the subject—such as a legendary hero, an inaccessible celebrity, or a literary figure—the relationship remains stable and is classified as external mediation (the red). In this state, the subject openly acknowledges the model and strives to emulate them without any risk of direct competition. However, when the mediator occupies the same social sphere as the subject, the dynamic transforms into internal mediation (the black). Because both individuals are now capable of pursuing the exact same object, the mediator simultaneously acts as a model to be imitated and a formidable rival to be defeated. This proximity breeds intense jealousy, secrecy, and resentment, as the subject is forced to hide their imitation while furiously competing for the identical prize.

As this rivalry within internal mediation intensifies, a profound psychological shift occurs, propelling the framework from a structural geometry of borrowed longing into the realm of metaphysical desire. Initially, the subject's attention is entirely fixated on the physical object itself, while the mediator is merely viewed as an obstacle standing in the way of acquisition. However, as the competition escalates, the object gradually loses its intrinsic value and recedes into the background, becoming little more than an arbitrary pretext for the conflict. The subject's obsession pivots completely away from the object and locks entirely onto the mediator. The rival, initially just a model, becomes a looming, omnipotent figure in the mind of the subject, endowed with an almost divine aura. The struggle is no longer about acquiring a specific, tangible prize; it is about confronting the mediator's perceived superiority.

From the perspective of the desiring subject, this shift is profoundly ontological. The subject feels acutely aware of their own internal emptiness, sensing a deep-seated lack of being or authenticity. Looking at the mediator, who appears fiercely autonomous and self-assured, the subject projects a mythical fullness onto this rival. The subject becomes convinced that the mediator possesses a hidden, transcendent quality—a metaphysical essence—that makes them complete and untouchable. The object of desire is now pursued not for its physical utility or beauty, but because it is seen as a tangible emanation of the mediator's divine essence. By acquiring the object, the subject secretly hopes to absorb the mediator's perceived fullness, thereby curing their own internal void. The geometry of imitation thus morphs into a desperate, magical quest to steal another human being's soul.

Ultimately, this pursuit of metaphysical essence traps the subject in a self-destructive cycle of perpetual enslavement. Because the perceived divine essence of the mediator is an illusion generated entirely by the subject's own mimetic fixation, it can never actually be acquired. Even if the subject successfully captures the disputed object, the anticipated ontological transfiguration fails to materialize; the object is immediately discarded as useless, and the subject's internal emptiness remains painfully intact. Driven by this agonizing failure, the subject seeks out ever more insurmountable rivals and increasingly punishing defeats, convinced that only a model who can consistently thwart them must truly possess the authentic essence they crave. The subject willingly subjugates themselves to the mediator, transforming their imitation into a grotesque form of religious worship where the rival is simultaneously idolized as a god and hated as an executioner.

To fully capture this dynamic, Girard vigorously opposes the romanesque to the romantique. In his terminology, a romantique work clings to the illusion of spontaneous desire, cloaking the imitative reality of human longing in myths of authentic passion, individual autonomy, and heroic isolation. Conversely, a romanesque work shatters this facade, brutally disclosing the triangular, borrowed nature of desire and exposing the protagonist's enslavement to a mediator. By defining these terms not merely as literary eras but as fundamental existential postures toward truth, Girard radically stretches the definition of the romantique. In his framework, this umbrella expands far beyond nineteenth-century poetry to include modern existentialism and even the philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche. Despite his fierce anti-idealism, Nietzsche still desperately clings to the illusion of the fiercely autonomous, self-generating individual, remaining completely blind to the underlying mechanics of mimetic rivalry that govern human behavior.

div.head: 3.2 David and Dickie.
div.p: The psychological need for mediation in the romanticTo avoid misunderstandings, we shall henceforth use the English word romantic in its basic modern meaning of relating to the emotional/sexual entanglement between two human beings and will use the French romantique for Girard's expanded literary category. life of David (the future King Edward VIII) strongly mirrors the internal architecture analyzed by Girard in his reading of Fyodor Dostoevsky's short novel The Eternal Husband. In Dostoevsky's tale, the character Pavel Pavlovich is completely incapable of desiring his own wife—or any other woman—without the validating presence of a mediator, specifically his wife's former lover, Velchaninov. The eternal husband is drawn to the lover with a magnetic, almost slavish devotion, desperately needing the rival's approving gaze to infuse the object of his affection with value.

David operated under an identical mechanism of internal mediation. Despite his supreme social standing as the Prince of Wales, he lacked the internal autonomy to spontaneously desire a partner. He was utterly dependent on a model to validate his romantic pursuits. For David, this model was his younger cousin, Lord Louis Dickie Mountbatten. Dashing, hyper-competent, and effortlessly charming, Dickie possessed the ontological fullness that David felt he intrinsically lacked. Consequently, David required Dickie to pre-approve and mediate his desire, transforming his younger cousin into a necessary third point in his romantic geometry.

This dependency was explicitly documented in David's own private correspondence. Writing to his then-mistress, Freda Dudley Ward, during a 1920 royal tour of the Caribbean, David complained bitterly about the women he was expected to dance with and revealed the structural role his cousin played in his private life. He confessed, I’ve appointed Dickie [Mountbatten] my procurer of partners & only take on a young woman that he has vetted...Andrew Lownie, The Mountbattens: Their Lives and Loves (London: Blink Publishing, 2019), p. 42. This extraordinary admission lays bare the mimetic nature of his desire: a woman only became romantically viable to the Prince once she had been processed through the approving gaze of his chosen mediator.

In Deceit, Desire and the Novel, Girard diagnoses this exact pathology, noting how the subject, desperate to maintain the illusion of the mediator's divine essence, actively engineers situations where the rival is forced to intercede. The subject practically thrusts the object of desire into the rival's path. As Girard observes regarding Dostoevsky's eternal husband:

cit.quote: The subject is torn between two opposite feelings toward his model—the most submissive reverence and the most intense malice. This is the passion of the Eternal Husband... he plays the part of a procurer.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 45.

div.p: This profound lack of autonomous desire dictated not only who vetted his partners, but the marital status of the partners themselves. Beyond his reliance on Dickie as a procurer, David's dependence on an outside mediator manifested in his systematic pattern of choosing married women as mistresses—a pattern clearly illustrated by his long-term affairs with Freda Dudley Ward, Lady Furness, and ultimately Wallis SimpsonPhilip Ziegler, King Edward VIII: The Official Biography (London: Collins, 1990), p. 224.. In the Girardian framework, a married woman inherently comes with a built-in mediator: her husband. Just as Dostoevsky's eternal husband could only desire a woman already validated by a lover, David could only pursue a woman whose value was socially guaranteed by her legal possession by another man. The husband served as the necessary rival whose prior claim to the object sparked the Prince's mimetic interest, confirming that his romantic engagements were never spontaneous, but strictly mediated by a third party.

As the mimetic disease progresses, the role of the mediator shifts from a mere vetting agent into an absolute, tyrannical master. The subject becomes addicted not to the validation of the model, but to the rejection and disdain that the model inevitably projects. The subject deliberately seeks out mediators who will dominate and humiliate them, because only a rival capable of inflicting such absolute defeat seems to possess the transcendent, divine autonomy the subject craves. Girard explains this descent into sado-masochism:

cit.quote: We no longer choose our mediator because of the admiration which he inspires in us but because of the disgust we seem to inspire in him.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 178.

div.p: This terrifying trajectory found its ultimate culmination in David's relationship with Wallis Simpson. Wallis perfectly embodied the impossibly dominant, dismissive mediator that David's worsening mimetic pathology required. Far from the warm, submissive archetype expected of a royal consort, she was notoriously abrasive, controlling, and openly contemptuous of him. She assumed the role of the ultimate obstacle and executioner. David's absolute, groveling submission to her—which famously led him to abdicate the throne of the British Empire—was not an act of supreme romantic love, as the romantique myth-makers would have it. Instead, his subjugation to Wallis verged entirely on the sado-masochistic; it was the logical endpoint of metaphysical desire, exactly as Girard predicts for a subject hopelessly enslaved to the divinity of their mediator.

div.head: 3.3 Virginia Woolf's bipolar disorder.
div.p: To fully grasp the psychological architecture of the Bloomsbury Group, one must re-examine the tragic trajectory of its central literary figure, Virginia Woolf. Historically, her profound psychological instability—often characterized today as bipolar disorder—is viewed as a purely clinical pathology or a biological inevitability intrinsically linked to her creative genius. However, when analyzed through the lens of mimetic desire, this supposed mental illness reveals a fundamentally different etiology. Rather than a solitary affliction, her violent mood swings were the structural consequences of intense, unresolved internal mediation. Her suffering was not generated ex nihilo from within her own biology; it was the agonizing manifestation of metaphysical desire, driven by the relentless, invisible gravity of the social models she simultaneously worshipped and despised.

The psychiatrist Jean-Michel Oughourlian, closely expanding upon Girard's framework, provides the exact diagnostic mechanism for this manic-depressive cycle. Oughourlian argues that these extreme emotional oscillations are directly tethered to the subject's shifting relationship with their mediator. The manic highs do not represent spontaneous bursts of chemical euphoria, but rather what he terms the élan vers le médiateur (the rush toward the mediator). During this phase of psychological inflation, the subject experiences a fleeting, intoxicating illusion of having successfully merged with the model and absorbed their divine essence. Oughourlian explains this euphoric apex:

cit.quote: The manic phase corresponds to a triumphant appropriation of the model's being. The subject experiences an exalting inflation of the ego, convinced that the void has finally been filled by the mediator's essence.
cit.bibl: Jean-Michel Oughourlian, The Puppet of Desire: The Psychology of Hysteria, Possession, and Hypnosis (Stanford: Stanford University Press, 1991), p. 162.

div.p: Unlike the romantic dependency of David Windsor, Woolf's mimetic cycles were not primarily tethered to sexual or romantic relationships. In her youth, her early depressive episodes were brutally triggered by the deaths of the family members she intensely idolized, most notably her mother, Julia Stephen, and her half-sister, Stella. In the Girardian framework, these figures functioned as her earliest, most powerful mediators of being. When they vanished, the source of her borrowed ontological fullness abruptly disappeared, violently plunging her into the void. As she transitioned into adulthood, this mimetic dependency shifted away from familial figures and became almost mechanically tethered to her professional writing activity and her fierce rivalries within the literary world.

When working on a new novel, Woolf would enter a manic phase of élan vers le médiateur. During the composition process, she felt she was ascending to the divine heights of her external mediators—transcendent literary idols such as Marcel Proust and Jane Austen. More urgently, writing offered the illusion that she was finally conquering her internal mediators, particularly her ex-fiancé Lytton Strachey and E.M. Forster, both of whom had achieved major literary successes before she did. Immersed in her work, she experienced a soaring conviction that she was absorbing their genius and becoming a literary goddess herself. Her diaries frequently capture this competitive exaltation, revealing how her manic highs were directly fueled by the need to outshine her peers. Recognizing this intense mimetic rivalry, her biographer Hermione Lee observes:

cit.quote: Her ambition was fiercely competitive. She was driven by an anxious, jealous need to measure herself against her contemporaries, especially Lytton Strachey and Morgan Forster... Writing was her mechanism for superiority; while deep in a draft, she felt a soaring, almost divine power that placed her above them all.
cit.bibl: Hermione Lee, Virginia Woolf (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1997), p. 342.

div.p: However, the moment the manuscript was completed and sent to the printers, this artificial mimetic high evaporated, triggering a catastrophic psychological crash. Without the active, daily process of writing to sustain the illusion that she was successfully appropriating her mediators' essence, Woolf was violently thrown back into her own internal emptiness. The printed book, now a mere physical object detached from the creative frenzy, failed to deliver the anticipated ontological transfiguration. She realized she had not become a permanent literary goddess; she was simply the same old boring Virginia as before, and severe depression inevitably ensued. She explicitly documented this agonizing post-publication plunge into the void in her own diary:

cit.quote: I have a feeling of my own incompetence and failure. I am the same old Virginia, writing the same old stuff. The book is out, and the illusion of my own power is shattered. I am left with nothing but this awful blankness, this sense of being an ugly, incompetent, and entirely useless woman.
cit.bibl: Virginia Woolf, The Diary of Virginia Woolf, Vol. III: 1925-1930 (London: Hogarth Press, 1980), p. 112.

div.p: In the literary establishment, portraying Woolf's despair strictly as a medical condition serves a powerful, deeply romantique purpose. By framing her suffering as an organic pathology inherent to the sublime but tormented writer, the cultural myth-makers protect the illusion of her fierce, solitary autonomy. To admit that her internal life was dictated by slavish imitation and desperate attempts to steal the essence of her peers would completely destroy the myth of the independent, self-generating artist. Girard fiercely diagnoses this protective maneuver, noting how the modern intellect desperately conceals its mimetic enslavement behind the mask of individualistic originality:

cit.quote: The romantic vaniteux always wants to convince himself that his desire is written into the nature of things, or, if that is impossible, that it is the emanation of a serene subjectivity, the creation ex nihilo of a quasi-divine ego.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 15.

div.p: This pattern of mimetic enslavement was in no way unique to Woolf; it was the defining architecture of the entire Bloomsbury Group. Beneath their carefully curated public facade of aristocratic ease and bohemian liberation, the collective functioned as a claustrophobic incubator of the black—the most toxic form of internal mediation. Their famously entangled affairs, open marriages, and constant sexual transgressions were not expressions of authentic free love or progressive enlightenment. Instead, they were brutal, covert status maneuvers executed to capture each other's metaphysical essence and inflict ontological defeat upon their rivals. The nervous breakdowns, vicious infighting, and collective despair that relentlessly haunted the group were the exact structural consequences of a community hopelessly trapped in an inescapable web of metaphysical desire.

div.head: 3.4 Apocalypse in Kenya.
div.p: The Happy Valley Set in colonial Kenya provides a perfect historical embodiment of the terminal stage of metaphysical desire. While they initially framed their behavior as an aristocratic assertion of ease, the escalating cycle of wife-swapping, substance abuse, and sadomasochistic psychological warfare inevitably collapsed into bloodshed. This trajectory perfectly illustrates what René Girard terms the Apocalypse dostoïevskienne (Dostoyevskyan apocalypse). In this final stage, the superficial differences between models and subjects dissolve completely, leaving only raw, undifferentiated mimetic rivalry.

In the isolated hothouse of the Wanjohi Valley, the colonial elite lived in a state of hyper-proximity, structurally implementing the type of situation Girard calls the black. As their transgressive rituals intensified, the objects of desire—primarily their sexual partners—lost all intrinsic value. They became mere tokens in an endless, agonizing contest for metaphysical supremacy. The constant circulation of spouses did not generate the promised aristocratic liberation; instead, it erased all individual boundaries. Everyone became a monstrous double of everyone else, locked in a cycle of reciprocal hatred and idolatry where the pursuit of the mediator's essence yielded nothing but universal emptiness.

As the geometry of internal mediation collapses upon itself, the framework reaches its breaking point. When the disputed objects finally disappear entirely from the subject's field of vision, only the furious, mesmerizing struggle between identical rivals remains. Girard diagnoses this ultimate descent into chaos as the moment when the romantic illusions of autonomy are completely shattered by the sheer gravity of reciprocal violence:

cit.quote: In the Dostoyevskyan apocalypse, the object of desire completely disappears, and the rivals are left entirely to their own reciprocal fascination. The destruction of the mediator becomes the only possible outcome for a subject entirely consumed by the model's perceived divinity.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 210.

div.p: This theoretical apocalypse became a bloody reality with the 1941 murder of Josslyn Hay, Lord Erroll. As the undisputed king of the Happy Valley Set, Erroll functioned as the ultimate, insurmountable mediator for the entire enclave. He was the local Nicolai StavroginIn René Girard's analysis of Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Possessed (or Demons), Nicolai Stavrogin serves as the supreme internal mediator. His chilling indifference and apparent total autonomy make him a magnetic idol for the surrounding characters, who project a divine ontological fullness onto him. Because all desires mimetically converge on this perfectly detached figure, the resulting rivalries trigger a catastrophic breakdown of the social order, culminating in the violent chaos that Girard terms the Dostoyevskyan apocalypse., possessing the supreme ontological fullness that the other colonists desperately craved. When Sir Jock Delves Broughton arrived in Kenya, he immediately fell into the fatal trap of internal mediation. Erroll brazenly seduced Broughton's younger wife, Diana, transforming the older man into the ultimate defeated subject. The subsequent probableOfficially, the murder of Lord Erroll remains unsolved, as Sir Jock Delves Broughton was tried and ultimately acquitted. The colonial police investigation was severely hampered by the very nature of Erroll's mimetic dominance: because he had systematically entangled himself in affairs, the enclave was filled with a massive pool of potentially jealous husbands and scorned lovers, obscuring the inquiry with too many plausible suspects. assassination of Erroll by Broughton was not a standard crime of romantic passion; it was a desperate, metaphysical strike to destroy the tyrannical model who had completely absorbed his being.

The aftermath of the murder permanently stripped away the enclave's romantique myths of effortless bohemian freedom, exposing the brutal, mechanical reality of their borrowed desires. The violent end of Lord Erroll perfectly demonstrates how the systematic destruction of societal boundaries—originally intended to forge an untouchable elite egregore—inevitably terminates in a sacrificial crisis. As James Fox summarizes the atmosphere surrounding the murder:

cit.quote: The fatal gunshot at the crossroads was not an isolated incident of jealousy, but the final, inevitable release of pressure in a closed social system that had fed entirely on the humiliation of its own members.
cit.bibl: James Fox, White Mischief: The Murder of Lord Erroll (New York: Random House, 1982), p. 284.

div.head: 3.5 Theurgical Metaphysics.
div.p: In Deceit, Desire, and the Novel, Girard frequently uses the adjective métaphysique in its traditional, slightly dismissive French connotation—implying a dynamic that has something to do with religion, illusion, and superstition (when he wants to show respect to religious notions, he uses transcendance). For Girard, the subject's quest is metaphysical because it chases an intangible, illusory essence rather than a concrete reality. However, the presence of Aleister Crowley in our historical sample set enables us to be significantly more precise. Crowley provides a technical, genuinely metaphysical, vocabulary for what Girard observes and depicts primarily in the language of psychological pathology.

As a traditional Western occultist, Crowley operates directly downstream of Neoplatonism and its ancient practice of theurgy. In the Platonic tradition, which constitutes the very foundation of Western metaphysics, the material world is sustained by a deeper, immaterial reality—its hypostasis or metaphysical underpinning. While traditional religion petitions the divine through passive prayer and acts of submission, theurgy seeks to actively manipulate this underlying architecture. It consists of highly specific ceremonial gestures and rituals designed to directly alter the fundamental essence of the cosmos.

Regardless of the extent to which Crowley personally believed in the objective reality of these forces, his framework of Sex Magick is explicitly represented as a series of theurgical acts. For Crowley, the transgressive sexual act is not merely a physical release or a psychological shock; it is a ceremonial technology. The sexual friction and orgiastic climax are engineered to generate and direct magical energy, altering the hypostatic layer of reality to manifest specific outcomes on the material plane. As the modern scholar Henrik Bogdan notes regarding this operational dynamic:

cit.quote: Crowley's sexual magick was fundamentally theurgical in nature. The sexual act was transformed into a highly formalized ritual designed to elevate the practitioner's consciousness and directly manipulate the divine forces governing the universe.
cit.bibl: Henrik Bogdan, Western Esotericism and Rituals of Initiation (Albany: State University of New York Press, 2007), p. 122.

div.p: At the core of this theurgical ambition lies the absolute supremacy of the Will. Much like Friedrich Nietzsche, who philosophically centered his cosmos around the Will to Power, Crowley gives center stage to the True Will of the individual. In this occult paradigm, theurgy provides the ultimate mechanical handle for the individual to bend the entire cosmos to his desires. The practitioner ceases to be a passive subject of divine providence and instead assumes the role of a sovereign creator, imposing their own will upon the fabric of existence. Crowley unequivocally stated this central tenet:

cit.quote: Magick is the Science and Art of causing Change to occur in conformity with Will... Every intentional act is a Magickal Act.
cit.bibl: Aleister Crowley, Magick in Theory and Practice (Paris: Lecram Press, 1929), p. 12.

div.p: This exact ambition to bend the cosmos to one's will perfectly describes the sociological and psychological behavior of the decadent British aristocrats we have discussed. Groups like the Bloomsbury Group and the Happy Valley Set belonged to the first generation of the British elite to have largely abandoned the orthodox Christian faith of their Victorian parents. Bereft of a God-given, external moral order to submit to and lean on, they found themselves staring into a terrifying ontological void. They were left with only one dizzying option to stave off existential despair: they had to attempt to control the cosmos entirely by their own power.

To achieve this impossible metaphysical sovereignty, they needed an operational power source. Like Crowley, they intuitively sought the required theurgic energy in the mysterious, dark aura of transgressive sex. By shattering the sexual taboos of the previous generation, they believed they were harvesting a sacred, liberating life force that would elevate them above the common masses. However, as Girard's framework reveals, this dark aura contains no actual magic. The intoxicating energy they sought during their sexual rituals was nothing more than the phantom of the mediator's perceived divinity—a mimetic mirage generated by their own intense rivalry. As Girard concludes on the true nature of this metaphysical illusion:

cit.quote: The subject is convinced that the mediator possesses a divine quality which he himself lacks... he expects this being to confer upon him the mastery of the universe. He seeks a transfiguration through the object, but the magic is only the projection of his own enslaved desire.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 53.

div.p: When the inevitability of this unfillable void is fully grasped, following the revelation of the Apocalypse dostoïevskienne, Suicide looms. David Windsor very nearly suicided the British monarchy and certainly his own Royal status. Woolf opted out when she realized the War had put an end to her fantasies by ushering in a more serious era of genuine danger. Broughton committed an act that was near suicidal. It is mere luck that he did not get caught. In spirit, what he did was a murder-suicide, the typical Dostoyevskyan-Girardian apocalyptic act.

div.head: 3.6 The Irresistible Attraction of the Frat Sex Ritual.
div.p: We are now in a better position to answer our initial question: What is it that Jane Doe hoped to achieve by walking into the Chi Phi frat house that night? Like hapless David Windsor, the Crowleyan ritualist or the frantic Kenyan wife-swappers, she was desperate to appropriate the theurgic energy of the sex magic act. She hoped that the divine quality of the mediator Chads was going to be transferred to her, through her physical submission. In Girard's framework, this dynamic is perfectly encapsulated in the figure of la coquette, a now old-fashioned term in French loosely applied to any woman overly enamoured of her own sex appeal. Girard explains that la coquette turns her own body into the very object of her mimetic longing, requiring the desire of her socially superior mediators to validate her own existence:

cit.quote: The coquette's indifference is not feigned... She desires herself. But she is incapable of desiring herself without the help of her lover. She uses the other's desire to desire herself... She offers her body to the other's desire in order to capture his divinity.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 105.

div.p: By willingly inserting her body into the highly formalized, multi-partner hieros gamos of the frat house, Jane Doe was engaging in a desperate, metaphysical maneuver. She was attempting to cure her own ontological emptiness by becoming the central object of desire for a collective of high-status male mediators. By engaging publicly in an act of visible desire under the watchful eye of here sorority sisters operating in the Black (where every disclosure of longing is cause for immediate scornful execution), she also committed reputational suicide, just like David Windsor

The modern Frat House is a homogenized, simplified, McDonald's-ified version of Crowley's Sicilian Abbey of Thelema. Cooked-up by still juvenile upper-class ex-OSS operatives, impressed to their core by Brit wartime decadent aristocratic glamour, when they resumed their Ivy-league studies or attended Alumni parties, the frat hieros gamos then followed the inevitable path of anything American post-war: democratized comodification. The modern frat house is built around the ritual. It exists solely for that purpose. In countless American Universities, not only in the Ivy league now, the McThelema frat house sits like an immoveable piece of Americana. For many, it is the real motivation for going to University after the High-School prolegomena: participating in the grand celebration of American masculine ambiguity, the consecration of king Chad.

This conclusion, though helpful, is not enough. To fully understand the phenomenon of frat orgiastic sex, we now need to delve into the vast submerged iceberg of historical elaboration of which it is but the tiny emerged top. As we have seen, the object of desire in the Girardian framework may be non-sexual (e.g. literary glory in the case of Woolf), while it may not be (by definition) in Crowleyan sex magick. This discrepancy indicates that further investigation is required. The best place to conduct an inquiry of this kind is longue dureé History, where enduring patterns can be stripped of accidental fluctuations. This is what we are going to do in the subsequent chapters.
